- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.4) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect upward — reduce forecast peak by 5–10% relative to recent highs.
- If model shows sharp upward spike followed by forecast overshoot, apply downward bias correction for next 3–5 periods, especially if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive.
- In cases where true outcome exceeds forecast by >10% over 3–5 periods, check if sentiment was positive recently — if so, model may be underestimating bullish momentum; adjust upward slightly but avoid overcorrection.
- If model consistently underestimates true values in early periods of a 30d forecast (e.g., first 5–7 days), apply a small upward bias (e.g., +2–5%) to compensate for lag.
- When sentiment is positive but model forecast is flat or declining, consider mean reversion bias — slightly increase forecast to reflect sentiment-driven momentum.
- If sentiment history shows repeated negative spikes followed by recovery, model often fails to capture the rebound — adjust forecast to include a 2–3 period lagged recovery signal.
- Avoid overreacting to single-day sentiment spikes — if sentiment shifts sharply, wait 2–3 periods before adjusting forecast unless price is already trending strongly.
- In high volatility periods (e.g., sentiment swings >0.3), reduce forecast smoothness — allow for ±3–5% deviation from historical mean to capture sentiment-driven noise.
